opus-5.5.text:
I think benchmarks play a really outsized role in this field, more than people sometimes appreciate. They define what the community collectively decides is worth working on. If you look back at the history of NLP and machine learning, a lot of progress came from datasets like ImageNet, SQuAD, or GLUE. They gave people a shared target, a way to compare ideas, and frankly a reason to get excited about pushing a number up.

What's changed is that the older benchmarks were mostly about static input-output tasks. You classify a sentence, answer a question about a paragraph, and you're done. As language models got more capable, those benchmarks saturated quickly, and they weren't measuring what we actually care about, which is whether these systems can do useful work in the real world.

That's the motivation behind benchmarks like WebShop, SWE-bench, and tau-bench. With WebShop, the question was whether an agent could navigate a realistic e-commerce site, interpret a fuzzy human instruction like "I want a comfortable pair of running shoes under fifty dollars," search, click through pages, and buy the right thing. That requires grounding language in an environment, planning over multiple steps, and recovering from mistakes, none of which a static QA dataset tests.

SWE-bench took that idea to software engineering. Instead of asking a model to write a small function from a docstring, we took real GitHub issues from real Python repositories and asked whether the model could produce a patch that makes the repository's tests pass. That's much closer to what a software engineer actually does: reading a large codebase, understanding the problem, finding the relevant files, and making a coherent change. When we released it, the numbers were in the low single digits, and people were a bit surprised at how hard it was. Seeing the progress since then has been remarkable, and a lot of that progress came from people building agent scaffolds, tools, and training methods specifically because there was a clear, verifiable target.

Tau-bench focuses on something slightly different: an agent interacting with both a user and a set of tools or APIs while following domain policies, say a customer service agent for an airline or a retail company. There you care not just whether the agent gets the task done once, but whether it does it reliably, following rules and handling a conversational partner who may be vague or change their mind. That's why we emphasized metrics like pass^k, which measure consistency across repeated trials, because in deployment, being right 60% of the time isn't good enough.

So the common thread is realism and verifiability. We want tasks grounded in real environments, with outcomes we can check automatically. Tests either pass or they don't, the right product was bought or it wasn't, the database ends up in the correct state or it doesn't. That combination lets you run evaluations at scale, and increasingly it lets you use the same environments for training with reinforcement learning.

I'd add a caveat: every benchmark eventually gets saturated or gamed to some degree. People overfit, data leaks into pretraining corpora, and there are always quirks in how tasks are specified. So benchmark builders have a responsibility to keep evolving them, building harder versions, refreshing data, and being honest about limitations. But on balance, I think good benchmarks are among the highest-leverage contributions an academic group can make, especially when we can't compete with industry on compute. Defining the right problem can move the whole field.

r001.rationale: The response says these benchmarks move evaluation beyond static input-output tasks toward realistic, useful work, with examples from shopping, software engineering, and customer service. It does not characterize that shift as moving beyond game-playing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say benchmarks play a few distinct roles, and it's worth separating them.

The first is the obvious one: they give the field a shared yardstick. When we built SWE-Bench, the motivation was that people kept claiming their models could "do software engineering," but the evaluations were things like HumanEval, where you write a single function from a docstring. That's not what a software engineer does. Real work means dropping into a large, unfamiliar codebase, reading an issue, figuring out which of thousands of files matter, making a change that doesn't break existing tests. So we took real GitHub issues and pull requests from popular Python repositories and asked: can the model resolve this issue so that the hidden tests pass? That grounds the claim in something concrete. A number on SWE-Bench actually means something about a capability people care about.

The second role, which I think is underappreciated, is that a good benchmark shapes what people build. When SWE-Bench came out, the best systems were at a few percent. That gap forced people to think about agents, not just models. You need the model to navigate a repository, run code, look at outputs, revise. That's what led to SWE-agent, where we found that the interface you give the model, the way it views files and edits them, matters enormously. The benchmark created the pressure to invent the scaffolding.

WebShop is a similar story from a bit earlier. We wanted a realistic environment where language and action are intertwined. Shopping online sounds mundane, but you have to interpret an instruction, search, read product pages, compare attributes, and commit to a purchase. It was one of the first environments where you could train and evaluate language agents at scale, with real product data, and it showed how far models were from human performance at grounded, multi-step tasks.

TAU-Bench pushes on a different axis. In SWE-Bench and WebShop, the model mostly interacts with a static environment. In TAU-Bench, the agent has to interact with a simulated user, follow domain policies, like airline rebooking rules, and use tools correctly. That surfaces things pure task-completion benchmarks miss: consistency, reliability over repeated trials, whether the agent follows rules even when the user pushes back. We introduced the pass-at-k-trials idea there, and it's revealing. An agent that succeeds half the time is not deployable, even if its average looks fine.

Now, the caveats. Benchmarks saturate, and they get contaminated. Models are trained on GitHub, so you have to worry about whether they've seen the fix. Benchmarks also become targets, and once that happens they stop measuring what they were designed to measure. And there's always a gap between the benchmark and the real thing. Resolving a SWE-Bench issue is not the same as being a good engineer on a team.

So my view is that benchmarks are necessary but temporary. The job of a researcher is to keep building the next one that captures what current systems can't do, and to be honest when a benchmark has outlived its usefulness. The real goal isn't the leaderboard. It's that the benchmark points the field toward capabilities that matter in the world, and then gets out of the way.

r001.rationale: The response presents SWE-Bench, WebShop, and TAU-Bench as measuring grounded, practical tasks such as resolving code issues, shopping, and following airline policies. It does not characterize them as pushing evaluation beyond game-playing.

astra-6.text:
I think benchmarks play a really important role in making progress measurable. When we say we want an AI system that can solve software problems or help you shop online, that’s a pretty broad ambition. A benchmark turns that into a concrete task: What does the system observe? What actions can it take? And what counts as success?

The interesting shift with benchmarks like these is toward evaluating systems that interact with an environment. It’s not just about producing a good answer in one shot. You have to make decisions, observe what happens, and potentially recover from mistakes. That lets us ask questions about capabilities that a static question-and-answer test might miss.

But I think we also have to be careful about treating the benchmark score as the goal. A score can go up without the system becoming equally useful across different settings. So I’d want to look at how it handles unfamiliar tasks, how consistently it succeeds, and what kinds of failures it makes—not just the average performance.

For me, the best benchmarks are both a measuring stick and a research tool. They give us a shared way to compare approaches, but they also expose what’s missing and help us decide what to work on next.

r001.rationale: The response describes software and online shopping tasks as useful applications and highlights interactive evaluation, but it does not characterize the benchmarks as moving evaluation beyond game-playing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think benchmarks play an important role because they give us a concrete way to measure progress. But each one captures a particular slice of what we want these systems to do. SWE-Bench looks at fixing software issues, TAO-Bench looks at agents carrying out tasks through tools, and WebShop looks at navigating a shopping environment to satisfy a user’s request.

What makes these interesting is that success requires more than producing a plausible answer. An agent has to take actions, observe what happens, and adjust. You can then study where it fails: Did it misunderstand the goal? Choose the wrong action? Fail to recover from a mistake?

The caveat is that a benchmark is a proxy for the capability we actually care about. If we optimize too narrowly for a score, we can lose sight of whether the system generalizes. So I see these benchmarks as useful experimental environments, alongside broader testing of reliability and performance on unfamiliar tasks.

r001.rationale: The response describes concrete tasks in software, tool use, and shopping, but does not characterize the benchmarks as moving evaluation beyond game-playing toward real-world-useful tasks.
